### Provide a description that is worded well enough to be understood

I extract Waterfox cookies for downloads, but either through Waterfox itself or through using my account on a different device (or YouTube just getting tired of me hitting so many videos in a row with the exact same auth cookies), the cookies go bad. I know this because I start seeing floods of:

`WARNING: [youtube] The provided YouTube account cookies are no longer valid. They have likely been rotated in the browser as a security measure.`

While some more videos often download after this, eventually the entire session falls into a 403 black hole, either never starting the stream downloads or abruptly stopping, sometimes leaving behind partials but mostly not. However, if I hit CTRL+C and immediately re-run the command, all the cookie notices vanish and several more videos download before the same trap springs. **Adding sleep intervals DOES NOT solve the problem, and usually results in less videos being downloaded per attempt.**

Since yt-dlp obviously is able to detect the failure condition, I propose that the program extracts cookies from the browser again upon noticing the condition and then resumes the playlist/tab download process, restarting the extraction for the current video and resuming from partials if required.

### Provide a description that is worded well enough to be understood

Apparently, at least one commercially available HLS packager generates .m3u8 files that refer to subtitle playlists without an extension.

Those .m3u8 files look somewhat like this:

```
#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:7
#EXT-X-INDEPENDENT-SEGMENTS
#EXT-X-MEDIA:TYPE=AUDIO,GROUP-ID="AACL",NAME="audio_482_deu",LANGUAGE="deu",AUTOSELECT=YES,DEFAULT=YES,CHANNELS="2",URI="stuff.m3u8/Alter-audio_482_deu(482)"
#EXT-X-MEDIA:TYPE=AUDIO,GROUP-ID="AACL",NAME="audio_483_eng",LANGUAGE="eng",AUTOSELECT=YES,DEFAULT=NO,CHANNELS="2",URI="stuff.m3u8/Alter-audio_483_eng(483)"
#EXT-X-MEDIA:TYPE=SUBTITLES,GROUP-ID="subtitle",NAME="deu_0",LANGUAGE="deu",AUTOSELECT=YES,DEFAULT=NO,FORCED=NO,URI="stuff.m3u8/Vtt-deu_0(100)"
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1000000,CODECS="mp4a.40.2,avc1.4d401e",RESOLUTION=768x432,FRAME-RATE=25,AUDIO="AACL",SUBTITLES="subtitle"
stuff.m3u8/Level(1)
#EXT-X-I-FRAME-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=115195,CODECS="avc1.4d401e",RESOLUTION=768x432,URI="stuff.m3u8/Iframe(1)"
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=7200000,CODECS="mp4a.40.2,avc1.64002a",RESOLUTION=1920x1080,FRAME-RATE=50,AUDIO="AACL",SUBTITLES="subtitle"
stuff.m3u8/Level(2)
#EXT-X-I-FRAME-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=336245,CODECS="avc1.64002a",RESOLUTION=1920x1080,URI="stuff.m3u8/Iframe(2)"
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=96000,CODECS="mp4a.40.2",AUDIO="AACL",SUBTITLES="subtitle"
stuff.m3u8/Level(3)
```

When `yt-dlp` parses the .m3u8 file, the function `extract_media` in `yt_dlp/extractor/common.py` under the  `if media_type == 'SUBTITLES':` case runs `determine_ext(url)`.

When this runs with a "normal" URL like `https://server/path/stuff/Vtt-deu0(100).m3u8`, this determines an extension of "m3u8", and the following `if sub_info['ext'] == 'm3u8':` matches. This then eventually results in subtitles that are downloaded correctly.

However, because *here* the URL looks like `https://server/path/stuff.m3u8/Vtt-deu_0(100)`, `determine_ext` returns an extension of "unknown_video" and the download proceeds with "Invoking http downloader" to downloading "this link", which then downloads the playlist, not the subtitles.


I'm not sure if it is actually necessary to run `determine_ext` here, because we are already in a HLS stream and I woudln't know what other kind of extension could be used. Just to be safe I changed the call to `determine_ext` by adding a default value of "m3u8", resulting in the following diff:

```diff
diff --git a/yt_dlp/extractor/common.py b/yt_dlp/extractor/common.py
index 573a9c5a0..ee0fb0ca3 100644
--- a/yt_dlp/extractor/common.py
+++ b/yt_dlp/extractor/common.py
@@ -2292,7 +2292,7 @@ def extract_media(x_media_line):
                 url = format_url(media['URI'])
                 sub_info = {
                     'url': url,
-                    'ext': determine_ext(url),
+                    'ext': determine_ext(url, default_ext='m3u8'),
                 }
                 if sub_info['ext'] == 'm3u8':
                     # Per RFC 8216 §3.1, the only possible subtitle format m3u8
```

This makes it work for the streams that I tested and shouldn't break anything.

> 
>     3. Monitoring num ber of requests and timeouts between requests per each IP and blocking them when the threshold is overpassed
> 
>

### Provide a description that is worded well enough to be understood

The IAMF/Eclipsa Audio track is format 773 and yt-dlp supports downloading it. It would be nice if the default audio (if available) that is used when downloading a video is format 773 instead of format 251.This format is still pre-release but more info is available here https://www.flatpanelshd.com/focus.php?subaction=showfull&id=1739336996 . https://www.flatpanelshd.com/pictures/eclipsaaudioces_2_large.jpg is of a different vide but has debug info showing the codec id. I think only MP4 currently supports IAMF audio https://github.com/AOMediaCodec/iamf-tools/blob/main/docs/external/encoding_with_external_tools.md#merge-an-iamf-file-with-video-into-mp4-using-ffmpeg but I wasn't able to figure this out.

The IAMF audio file can be downloaded with:
`yt-dlp -f 773 'https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ItvQeAkpG-M'`
`yt-dlp -f 773 'https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CD7n92qPuq4'`

The downloaded m4a can be played with `ffplay`

        if not video.get('videoUrl'):

        formats, subtitles = self._extract_m3u8_formats_and_subtitles(
            video['videoUrl'], video_id, 'mp4', m3u8_id='hls')

        season = video.get('season')
        season_number = int_or_none(self._search_regex(

        episode = video.get('chapter')
        episode_number = int_or_none(self._search_regex(

        return {

            'title': video.get('title'),
            'description': next_data.get('long_description') or video.get('description'),

            'formats': formats,
            'subtitles': subtitles,

                'timestamp': ('sunrise_timestamp', {parse_iso8601}),
                'duration': ('duration', {float_or_none}),
                'categories': ('tags', {list}),

    def _report_errors(self, video):
        playability_errors = traverse_obj(video, ('playabilityErrors', ...))
        if not playability_errors:
            raise ExtractorError('No videoUrl and no information about errors')

        elif 'FSK_BLOCKED' in playability_errors:
            details = traverse_obj(video, ('playabilityErrorDetails', 'FSK_BLOCKED'), expected_type=dict)
            message = format_field(''.join((
                format_field(details, 'minEveningHour', ' from %02d:00'),
                format_field(details, 'maxMorningHour', ' to %02d:00'),
                format_field(details, 'minAge', ' (Minimum age %d)'),
            )), None, 'Only available%s') or 'Blocked by FSK with unknown availability'

        elif 'NOT_YET_AVAILABLE' in playability_errors:
            message = format_field(
                video, (('playabilityErrorDetails', 'NOT_YET_AVAILABLE', 'availableFrom'), 'currentSunrise'),
                'Only available from %s') or 'Video not yet available with unknown availability'

        else:
            message = f'Video unavailable: {", ".join(playability_errors)}'

        raise ExtractorError(message, expected=True)

I've currently set all my (network-related) retry parameters to `infinite`:
`--retries infinite --fragment-retries infinite`
Except for `--extractor-retries`, which is set to 10.
The reason for the second line's parameters is that I have a rather unstable internet connection which usually fixes itself after some time (I also have `--retry-sleep 3`). And the reason for `--extractor-retries 10` is the infamous "Incomplete data received" error in comments extraction which is believed to be a server-side issue. If I set `--extractor-retries` to `infinite`, I will never be able to get past the first "Incomplete data received" error.
This is a huge problem for people with bad internet connections such as me facing gigantic comment sections such as those in the example URLs. As I've established, setting `--extractor-retries infinite` is not an option when extracting comments, so a finite number has to be set.

And the download gets called.

The fact that comments extraction stops prematurely proves that finite retries are not feasible for people with bad connections. Theroratically one could set a huge number, and while that would probably *work*, it would take a terribly long time considering how often the "Incomplete data received" error happens.
And the fact that the subtitles eventually get downloaded also proves that infinite retries do eventually lead to download in most cases.

I believe I've explained the problem well enough, now for my two proposed solutions.

---

The first one is probably really easy and is what is described in the title. Making the "Incomplete data received" error into an entirely different error category and adding a corresponding retry option would solve this problem, as setting `--extractor-retries` to `infinite` would finally become feasible. However I believe this would be against the general structure of the project as comments extraction is extraction and thus any errors in it would be an extractor issue.

My second proposition is probably far more involved but would probably solve some other issues as well: adding comments resume.
This wouldn't *directly* solve this problem but simply running yt-dlp again after the user fixes their connection is far better than having to wait 30000 comments again. Not to mention there's a not small chance that their connection might break after those 30000 comments once more.

I did do some research around the issue tracker and found [this old comment](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/issues/380#issuecomment-855370022) by pukkandan:
> Do continuation tokens expire or otherwise become invalid after some time? If not, it is possible by treating comment extraction as a "fragment download" and writing each new "fragment" along with a `.ytdl` file with continuation token. But that would need a complete rewrite of the current comment extraction code

And coletdjnz [replied](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp/issues/380#issuecomment-855371600):
> > Do continuation tokens expire or otherwise become invalid after some time?
> 
> Not sure, we'd need to experiment with this.
> > If not, it is possible by treating comment extraction as a "fragment download" and writing each new "fragment" along with a .ytdl file with continuation token. But that would need a complete rewrite of the current comment extraction code
> 
> Hmm maybe. Also - if we were to implement something like that then we might want to make it work for other places where continuations are used (e.g. playlists) too.

Soooo... did this experimentation happen?

>Why Deno?
>
> Deno has a highly restrictive permission model by default and does not allow filesystem or network access. This is essential to protect our less-technically-inclined users. Implementing a built-in solution to this will also require JavaScript functionality which far exceeds that of our native jsinterp module. On Linux, I recommend using static quickjs with bubblewrap sandbox from flatpak.
/opt/qjs/qjs-sandboxed:
```
#!/bin/sh
script=""
for a in "$@"; do
  case "$a" in
    /tmp/tmp*/*) ;;
    /tmp/tmp*.js) script="$a" ;;
  esac
done

run() {
  exec bwrap \
    --unshare-all \
    --die-with-parent \
    --new-session \
    --cap-drop ALL \
    --clearenv \
    --tmpfs /tmp \
    --ro-bind /opt/qjs/qjs.original /opt/qjs/qjs.original \
    "$@"
}

if [ -n "$script" ] && [ -f "$script" ]; then
  run --ro-bind "$script" "$script" /opt/qjs/qjs.original "$@"
else
  run /opt/qjs/qjs.original "$@"
fi
```

In my case, the issue was resolved by installing a PO Token Provider.

For Windows:

Update yt-dlp:
python -m pip install -U yt-dlp
Install bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider:
python -m pip install -U bgutil-ytdlp-pot-provider
Install Deno and ensure it is available in your PATH.
Ensure yt-dlp-ejs is installed.
Run yt-dlp with verbose output:
yt-dlp -v "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SpjgknGiM2Q"

In my case, after installing and configuring the PO Token Provider, it was possible to download the video in 2160p (4K).

Your log shows:

[youtube] [pot] PO Token Providers: none

and:

web_creator client https formats require a GVS PO Token which was not provided

Therefore, it appears that the lack of a PO Token Provider might be the reason why higher-quality formats are unavailable.

The official yt-dlp guide on PO tokens recommends using a PO Token Provider instead of extracting the tokens manually.

`~/.local/bin/yt-dlp_linux --update-to nightly`
Then to get upgrades in the future:
`~/.local/bin/yt-dlp_linux -U`

Yesterday, I did some tests, on **Windows**; the **PSF**-offered, "official", CPython binaries for the python versions _currently supported_ by `yt-dlp`, py3.10+, together with the **OpenSSL** versions they ship with, are listed below:

CPython-3.**10**.11/OpenSSL-1.1.1**t**
CPython-3.**11**.9/OpenSSL-3.0.**13**
CPython-3.**12**.10/OpenSSL-3.0.**16**
CPython-3.**13**.9/OpenSSL-3.0.**18**
CPython-3.**14**.0/OpenSSL-3.0.**18**

Using _any_ CPython version of the **above set** to launch `yt-dlp` with a `rumble.com` "target" results in the unfortunate **403** block 😡 ...
So, it's safe to assume that both the `1.1.1*` (deprecated, at least for non-paying mere mortals) and `3.0.x` **LTS** branches of **OpenSSL** are being blocked by CF's anti-bot "protection" mechanism; NB that the `3.0.x` LTS branch hasn't yet been deprecated, as it's still supported for the next 9 months: 

https://endoflife.date/openssl

with `3.0.18` being the latest release...

Then, on a py3.**11** install, I continued my tests, with **manually updating its OpenSSL version**; this is relatively easy to do on **Windows**, as the PSF supply distinct/standalone OpenSSL dlls, files `libcrypto-3.dll+libssl-3.dll`, to be found inside the `DLLs` folder in the main installation directory (where `python.exe` resides); the relevant `_ssl.pyd` file (a "disguised" dll itself) allows for such manual upgrades via file-overwriting, but it doesn't allow one to downgrade to, say, the `1.x.x*` branches). 

My source of different and/or updated OpenSSL versions, for **Windows**, are mostly:
https://slproweb.com/products/Win32OpenSSL.html
https://wiki.overbyte.eu/wiki/index.php/ICS_Download (scroll down to "Download OpenSSL Binaries").
